procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 15, 1956, of the former Nagpur High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 205 of 1956 and Criminal Reference No. 15 of 1956, arising out of the judgment and order dated July 10, 1956 of the First Additional District Judge, Nagpur in Sessions Trial No. 34 of 1956.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The First Additional District Judge, Nagpur issued a judgment and order dated July 10, 1956 in Sessions Trial No. 34 of 1956. This was appealed to the Nagpur High Court, resulting in Criminal Appeal No. 205 of 1956 and Criminal Reference No. 15 of 1956. The Nagpur High Court then issued a judgment and order dated October 15, 1956.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the appellant challenged the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court notes that it does not ordinarily function as a Court of criminal appeal and that a High Court cannot grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a ground that is essentially one of fact.

issue.issue_text: Whether a High Court is competent under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a ground which is essentially one of fact.

facts: The appellant, convicted of murder, was granted a certificate of fitness to appeal to the Supreme Court by the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution.

The High Court granted the certificate on the grounds that there was 'not enough evidence against the accused' and that there was an error in its own judgment regarding the sufficiency of corroborating evidence for a dying declaration.
Essentially, the High Court granted the certificate based on a question of fact: whether there was sufficient evidence to prove the guilt of the accused.
law: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of criminal appeal.
Under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution, a High Court is not competent to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a ground which is essentially one of fact.
The Supreme Court only hears appeals on facts as a regular Court of Appeal in cases certified under clauses (a) or (b) of Article 134(1), not clause (c).
A certificate under Article 134(1)(c) should be granted only on a difficult question of law or procedure that requires settlement by the Supreme Court.
application: The Supreme Court examined the reasons given by the High Court for granting the certificate.
It found that the High Court did not grant the certificate based on any question of law or procedure, but rather on a question of fact, namely, the sufficiency of the evidence against the accused.
By granting the certificate on a factual ground, the High Court exceeded its power under Article 134(1)(c).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the certificate of fitness granted by the High Court was incompetent because it did not satisfy the requirements of Article 134(1)(c). The High Court cannot grant such a certificate on a ground that is essentially one of fact. Therefore, the appeal based on such a certificate had to be dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court ordinarily functions as a Court of Criminal Appeal to decide on questions of fact.

facts: In the case at hand, the High Court granted a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution.
The basis for the certificate was not a difficult question of law or procedure, but rather a question of fact: whether there was sufficient evidence to prove the guilt of the accused.
law: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of Criminal Appeal.
A High Court is not competent and exceeds its power under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution if it grants a certificate of fitness for appeal on a ground that is essentially a question of fact.

The Supreme Court does have the power and duty to hear appeals on facts, as a regular Court of Appeal, but only in cases coming to it on a certificate under Articles 134(1)(a) or (b) of the Constitution.
This principle was previously established in cases such as *Dey. v. The State of West Bengal* and *Narsing v. The State of Uttar Pradesh*.
application: The Court applied the established legal principle that it does not ordinarily decide on mere questions of fact in criminal appeals.

It determined that the High Court had improperly granted the certificate under Article 134(1)(c) because the certificate was based on a factual question (sufficiency of evidence) rather than a question of law requiring settlement by the Supreme Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the premise that it ordinarily functions as a Court of Criminal Appeal to decide on questions of fact. It held that its role is not to reconsider factual findings, and a High Court is not justified in granting a certificate for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) on a ground that is essentially one of fact.

issue.issue_text: Whether a dying declaration can, by itself, form the basis for a conviction.

law.fact_text: Under Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act, a statement made by a person as to the cause of their death is a relevant fact and an exception to the general rule against hearsay evidence.
law.relevant_text: The Legislature in its wisdom has enacted ins. 32(1) of the Evidence Act that "When the statement is made by a person as to the ca,,use of his death, or as to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death, in cases in which the cause of that person's death comes into question", such a statement written or verbal made by a person who is dead (omitting the unnecessary words) is itself a relevant fact. This provision has been made by the Legislature, advisedly, as a matter of sheer necessity by way of an exception to the general rule that hearsay is no evidence and that evidence, which has not been tested by cross-examination, is not admissible.

law.fact_text: A dying declaration is not considered a weaker kind of evidence than other forms of evidence and should not be equated with the testimony of an accomplice or a retracted confession, which may come from a tainted source.
law.relevant_text: it cannot be laid down as a general proposition that a dying declaration is a weaker kind of evidence than other pieces of evidence; (4) that a dying declaration stands on the same footing as another piece of evidence... Though under s.133 of the Evidence Act, it is not illegal to convict a person on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice... The same cannot be said of a dying declaration because a dying declaration may not, unlike a confession, or the testimony of an approver, come from a tainted source.

application.fact_text: The Court rejected the proposition that it is unsafe to convict solely on a dying declaration, stating there is no absolute rule of law or prudence that requires corroboration.
application.relevant_text: On a review of the relevant provisions of the Evidence Act and of the decided cases... we have come to the conclusion... (l) that it cannot be laid down as an absolute rule of law that a dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of conviction unless it is corroborated

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that the solemnity of the occasion, with the declarant facing imminent death, substitutes for the oath and the test of cross-examination, giving the statement a special sanctity.
application.relevant_text: In. the view of the Legislature, that test is supplied by the solemn pcca- sion when it was made, namely, at a time when the person making the statement was in danger of losing his life. At such a serious and solemn moment, that person is not expected to tell lies; and secondly, the test of cross-examination would not be available. In · such a case, the necessity of oath also has been dispensed with for the same reasons.

application.fact_text: The Court established that each case must be decided on its own facts. The reliability of a dying declaration must be assessed by considering the surrounding circumstances.
application.relevant_text: each case must be determined on its own facts keeping in view tbe circumstances in which the dying declara- tion was made

application.fact_text: To test the declaration's reliability, a court must consider factors such as the dying person's opportunity for observation, their mental capacity, the consistency of the statement, and the manner in which it was recorded.
application.relevant_text: in order to test the reliability of a dying declaration, the Court has to keep in view the circumstances like the opportunity of the dying man for observation, for example, whether there was sufficient light if the crime was committed at night; whether the capacity of the man to remember the facts stated had not been impaired at the time he was making the statement... that the statement has been consistent throughout

application.fact_text: If, after carefully considering all circumstances, the court is fully convinced that the dying declaration is true, it is the court's duty to convict, even without corroboration.
application.relevant_text: if the Court, after taking everything into consideration, is convinced that the statement is true, it is its duty to convict, not- withstanding that there is no corroboration in the true sense. The Court must, of course, be fully convinced of the truth of the statement

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a dying declaration can, by itself, form the basis for a conviction. The Court held that there is no absolute rule of law requiring corroboration for a dying declaration. Instead, each case must be judged on its own facts. If a court, after carefully scrutinizing the circumstances in which the declaration was made and assessing its reliability, is fully convinced of its truthfulness, it can and should base a conviction solely upon it.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a High Court is competent under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal to the Supreme Court on a ground which is essentially one of fact.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's position, by virtue of accepting and appealing on the basis of the certificate, is that the High Court was competent to grant it. The High Court's reasoning, which the appellant adopts, was that a factual error was discovered in its judgment (regarding the reason for the accused's absconding) and that the 'sufficiency of the evidence might be a matter for consideration in the light of this additional evidence,' making it a fit case for a certificate.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument, inferred from the court's judgment, is that the High Court was not competent to grant the certificate. The certificate was granted on a question 'which is essentially one of fact, namely, whether there was sufficient evidence of the guilt of the accused,' and not on a 'difficult question of law or procedure' as required for a valid certificate under Article 134(1)(c).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court ordinarily functions as a Court of Criminal Appeal to decide on questions of fact.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, by appealing on the basis of a certificate granted on the 'sufficiency of the evidence,' implicitly argued that the Supreme Court should re-examine the factual findings of the High Court, especially since the High Court itself expressed doubt.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, supported by the court's final decision, is that the Supreme Court does not ordinarily re-assess factual evidence or function as a regular court of criminal appeal on facts. The court's role is not to substitute its own assessment of evidence for that of the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a dying declaration can, by itself, form the basis for a conviction.
appellant_arguments: A dying declaration cannot be the sole basis for a conviction and requires corroboration. The appellant strongly relied on the Supreme Court's previous ruling in 'Ram Nath Madhoprasad v. State of Madhya Pradesh' as laying down a 'sound proposition of law' to this effect. It was also argued that the alleged absconding of the accused could not be used as sufficient corroboration.
respondent_arguments: A dying declaration can form the sole basis for a conviction without corroboration, provided the court is satisfied that it is true and reliable. The need for corroboration arises only if a court finds a particular dying declaration to be unreliable or suffering from an infirmity, not from any inherent weakness in this type of evidence. The observations in the 'Madhoprasad' case were in the nature of 'obiter dicta' and did not lay down a binding rule of law.

cases.case_name: Haripada Dey v. The State of West Bengal
cases.principle: A High Court exceeds its power under Art. 134(1)(c) of the Constitution if it grants a certificate of fitness for appeal based on a question of fact, as the Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of Criminal Appeal to decide mere questions of fact.

cases.case_name: Narsing v. The State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.principle: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of Criminal Appeal on questions of fact under a certificate granted under Art. 134(1)(c) of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not an absolute rule of law that a dying declaration must be corroborated by other independent evidence to form the sole basis of a conviction. If a court, after close scrutiny, is satisfied that the dying declaration is true and reliable, it can be acted upon without corroboration.
obiter: A dying declaration is not a weaker kind of evidence than other pieces of evidence and should not be placed in the same category as the evidence of an accomplice or a confession.
A dying declaration recorded by a competent magistrate in the form of questions and answers stands on a much higher footing than a dying declaration that depends on oral testimony.

To test the reliability of a dying declaration, the court must consider the circumstances in which it was made, such as the opportunity for observation, the declarant's capacity to remember, and the consistency of the statement.
The Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of criminal appeal.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal must be dismissed because the High Court's certificate of fitness under Article 134(1)(c) was incompetent, having been granted on a question of fact—the sufficiency of evidence—rather than a difficult question of law. The Supreme Court does not ordinarily function as a Court of Criminal Appeal to re-evaluate facts, and in any event, the legal premise of the appeal is flawed, as a dying declaration can form the sole basis for a conviction if the court is satisfied it is true, without any absolute requirement for corroboration.
legal_tests_applied: A certificate of fitness under Article 134(1)(c) is improperly granted if the main ground on which it was based related to a question of fact; it must be based on a 'difficult question of law or procedure'.

To assess a dying declaration, it must be 'very closely scrutinised, and tested as any other piece of evidence,' but 'once the Court comes to the conclusion, in any particular case, that it is true, no question of corroboration arises.'

There is 'no absolute rule of law, not even a rule of prudence that has ripened into a rule of law, that a dying declaration in order that it may sustain an order of conviction must be corroborated by other independent evidence.'
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's appeal was founded on a certificate of fitness that the Court deemed incompetent because the High Court 'exceeds its power of granting a certificate of fitness under that article if the certificate discloses that the main ground on which it was based related to a question of fact'.

The appellant was asking the Supreme Court to re-evaluate the sufficiency of evidence, a role the Court does not ordinarily undertake in such appeals, as it 'does not function, ordinarily, as a Court of Criminal Appeal' on mere questions of fact.

The appellant's primary legal argument, that a dying declaration requires corroboration based on the 'Madhoprasad' case, was rejected. The Court held that those observations 'are in the nature of obiter dicta and do not lay down the law.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld that the High Court's certificate was invalid because it was granted 'not on any difficult question of law or procedure... but on a question which is essentially one of fact, nemely, whether there was sufficient evidence of the guilt of the accused.'

The respondent's argument that a dying declaration can be the sole basis for conviction was accepted. The Court ruled that if a declaration is found to be true, 'no question of corroboration arises,' and it cannot be placed in the same category as evidence from an accomplice or a confession, which have inherent weaknesses.
The respondent successfully argued that the precedent cited by the appellant ('Madhoprasad') did not establish a binding rule of law requiring corroboration for all dying declarations.
policy_considerations: The Court reinforced the distinct constitutional roles of the High Courts and the Supreme Court, stating that the Supreme Court 'does not, ordinarily, concern itself with deciding mere questions of fact' on certificates of fitness, thereby preserving the finality of factual determinations by lower courts and managing its own appellate docket.

The Court affirmed the legislative policy behind Section 32(1) of the Indian Evidence Act, which makes a dying declaration an exception to the hearsay rule, noting that the 'special sanctity which the Legislature attaches to such a declaration must be respected' unless it is proven to be unreliable.
